title: Where a vLLM cold start goes
question: Where does a cold vLLM start on a rented GPU spend its time, and which empty cache is worth warming more: the weights or the compiled code? One of them also turned out to buy serving memory (KV cache).

requirements.short: Split the start into named phases
requirements.text: Split one cold start into named phases, and label what cannot be attributed instead of hiding it.
requirements.why: The caches act on different phases (weights on loading, compile on engine start), so one "startup" bar would hide half the experiment. Naming unattributed time is more credible than hiding it.

requirements.text: Change exactly one thing between the set-ups being compared.
requirements.why: Otherwise a difference cannot be pinned on a cache. Same image, entrypoint and engine flags for every arm.

requirements.short: Distribution and interval, not a mean
requirements.text: Report the distribution and its uncertainty, not an average.
requirements.why: Cold starts are skewed with a heavy tail, so a mean describes no real run. A claim like "cache X matters more" needs its own interval, not two point estimates side by side.

requirements.short: Fix the rules before the data
requirements.text: Fix the hypotheses, exclusion rules, stopping rule and headline rule before the first paid measurement run.
requirements.why: Git timestamps then show the rules came before the data, and the headline cannot be picked by which result cost the most effort.

requirements.text: Run only proven code on paid GPUs, and let anyone re-derive every number on a laptop.
requirements.why: The whole budget was $200, and debugging on live GPUs eats it. A number a reader cannot re-derive must be taken on trust.
requirements.unlinked_reason: It is met by process: the flow step "Capture, then build offline" tests the code against recorded fixtures and a free stub before paid runs, and "Publish what re-derives" re-derives every figure from the committed store with no GPU.

concepts.plain: Three cache set-ups. **A**: weights from the model hub, compile cache cold. **B**: weights from a network volume, compile cache cold. **C**: weights from the volume, compile cache warm. Background: P1, LLM serving.
One run of each arm, in an order shuffled from a seed. 100 triples make the 300 runs, so a busy hour on the fleet falls on all three arms.

A **contrast** is the difference of two arms' medians, with a bootstrap interval: A minus B is the weight cache's saving, B minus C the compile cache's. Their **difference**, (A minus B) minus (B minus C), ranks the caches only if its interval excludes zero; negative favours the compile cache.

concepts.term: Two clocks and the platform residual
concepts.plain: **Clock A** (laptop) brackets the whole job; total cold start is its span minus the worker-clock warmup after first token.**Clock B** (worker, monotonic) starts just before `vllm serve` is launched. **Platform time** = total minus clock B time, the one allowed cross-clock subtraction: queue, container start, handler set-up, teardown, polling lag. **Clock C**, RunPod's own queue and execution durations, is recorded but not used.
**p90** is the time 90% of runs finish within; p50 is the median. An **ECDF** plots every run (seconds across, share finished up), so the tail stays visible. More in P2.

**H1**: weight handling is over half of worker-clock time to first token (`T_process`) in arm A. **H2**: volume weights cut it materially. **H3**: compiling is a non-trivial part of engine start, and a warm cache cuts it. **H4**: host differences drive the median-to-p95 gap. **H5**: a warm compile cache leaves more KV cache.

Hypotheses, contrasts, exclusion rules, stopping rule and headline rule, committed in `docs/experiment.md` before any paid measurement run, four days before the published campaign's first run; later additions are dated in git.

decisions.title: Three arms, one variable
decisions.problem: Two caches start empty: the weights and the compiled code. To rank them, each comparison must change one thing only.
options: Two arms: hub vs volume weights
Add a baked-image arm, weights inside the container image
Add the fourth cell: weights cold, compile cache warm
One variable, cache configuration, at three levels: A, B, C
decisions.chosen: One variable, cache configuration, at three levels: A, B, C
decisions.why: A to B isolates the weight cache. B to C isolates the compile cache with weight handling held constant. The configuration is one frozen object that sets two paths, so the single-variable claim is true by structure. A baked image does not remove the bytes; it moves them into the image pull, which happens before any measuring code runs, so it would flatter the number for a reason the harness cannot see. Nobody warms a compile cache while re-downloading weights, so the fourth cell answers no question.
decisions.cost: Arm C exists only because the reconnaissance run showed this vLLM compiles at startup. A warm arm needs a primed volume, and a test has to check that the arms differ nowhere else.
decisions.why_short: A to B isolates the weight cache, B to C the compile cache; one frozen configuration makes the single-variable claim true by structure.
decisions.cost_short: Arm C needs a primed volume, and a test checks that the arms differ nowhere else.

serves.because: R2 asks to change exactly one thing; here cache configuration is one frozen object that sets two paths, "so the single-variable claim is true by structure".

uses.because: It chooses the three set-ups A, B and C that the concept defines.
"A to B isolates the weight cache. B to C isolates the compile cache": each adjacent pair of arms is one contrast.

decisions.title: Measure from outside the engine
decisions.problem: vLLM's interesting phases are internal, and part of every cold start (queue, container start, image pull) happens before our code exists.
options: Time startup through vLLM's Python engine API
One clock, and give all the time to the stages you can see
Run the real `vllm serve`, bracket it with a monotonic clock, split phases from its log, and get platform time by subtraction
decisions.chosen: Run the real `vllm serve`, bracket it with a monotonic clock, split phases from its log, and get platform time by subtraction
decisions.why: The Python API would measure a startup path nobody deploys. With one clock you cannot detect that it is lying. The design names three; the implemented check compares the driver and worker clocks and discards a run whose total leaves no room for a network round trip. The platform residual is the one named cross-clock subtraction; total time to first token is itself the job's laptop-clock span minus the worker-clock warmup tail.
decisions.cost: Platform time is one residual, and it holds teardown and polling lag as well as queueing. RunPod's queue and execution durations (clock C) are recorded but not used to split it. Two engine sub-phases (device init and KV allocation) are not delineated by this vLLM build, so they sit merged in an unattributed row. The log patterns are tied to vLLM 0.27.1.
decisions.why_short: Timing the real `vllm serve` from outside measures the path people deploy, and a second clock lets a lying run be caught.
decisions.cost_short: Platform time is one residual that also holds teardown and polling lag; two engine sub-phases stay merged.

serves.because: R1 asks for named phases and a label on what cannot be attributed; this decision splits phases from vLLM's log, names platform time as a residual, and puts the sub-phases the log does not delineate "in an unattributed row".

uses.because: It uses the driver and worker clocks, and platform time "is the one named cross-clock subtraction".

decisions.title: Interleave the arms in random triples
decisions.problem: A rented GPU fleet changes over hours and days. Run the arms in blocks and a busy evening gets labelled as an arm effect.
options: Blocks: all of A, then all of B, then all of C
Interleaved triples: one run of each arm per triple, order shuffled from a seed
decisions.chosen: Interleaved triples: one run of each arm per triple, order shuffled from a seed
decisions.why: Blocking confounds the cache with time-of-day fleet conditions, and on a rented fleet that confound can be large enough to make or erase the whole effect. The design calls interleaving its most important validity decision. Triples also allow a paired, same-host check as supporting evidence.
decisions.cost: A resumed campaign must rebuild the exact schedule, so the harness refuses a resume whose stored arms disagree with the seed. The windows ended up hours apart rather than on separate days, so drift between windows is only partly covered; the post says so.
decisions.why_short: Running all of one arm first would mix the cache effect with time-of-day fleet conditions.
decisions.cost_short: A resume must rebuild the exact schedule; drift between windows hours apart is only partly covered.

serves.because: R2's "one thing" covers when a run happens too: in blocks, fleet conditions change along with the arm, so "a busy evening gets labelled as an arm effect".

uses.because: The chosen option is "one run of each arm per triple, order shuffled from a seed".

decisions.title: Check each arm's cache state
decisions.problem: A warm cache leaking into a cold arm, or a cold compile inside arm C, would still produce plausible numbers. The configuration alone does not show what was on disk.
options: Let arm C's first campaign runs warm the cache
Prime arm C outside the campaign, isolate cold paths per run, and check the compile-cache state on every run
decisions.chosen: Prime arm C outside the campaign, isolate cold paths per run, and check the compile-cache state on every run
decisions.why: Without priming, arm C's early runs compile cold and later ones do not: a mixture whose effect grows with run index, which looks like a real trend. So two priming runs go to a separate store, and the second must show the cache present and compile under one second. Cold paths are named by run id so a reused worker cannot hand one run's files to another. The handler checks whether the compile cache exists before the engine starts, because a cold compile creates that directory as it finishes; a run whose observed state disagrees with its arm is discarded.
decisions.cost: Priming runs cost GPU time and are excluded from every number. Moving the check to after the engine run would look harmless but quietly discard about two thirds of a paid campaign, so the code carries a do-not-move warning.
decisions.why_short: Unprimed, arm C's early runs compile cold and later ones do not, which looks like a real trend.
decisions.cost_short: Priming runs cost GPU time and are excluded from every number.

serves.because: A warm cache leaking into a cold arm, or a cold compile inside arm C, would make the arms differ in more than their configured cache; "the configuration alone does not show what was on disk", so the compile-cache state is checked before every run, and cold weight paths are isolated per run.

uses.because: Each arm has an expected cache state, and "a run whose observed state disagrees with its arm is discarded".

decisions.title: Rank the caches by the difference's interval
decisions.problem: Which cache buys more? Two effects, each with its own interval, do not answer that.
options: Subtract the weight-time contrast from the compile-time contrast
Bootstrap the difference of contrasts on total cold start, and pick the headline by a rule fixed in advance
decisions.chosen: Bootstrap the difference of contrasts on total cold start, and pick the headline by a rule fixed in advance
decisions.why: "Compile cache mattered more" is only a finding if the gap between the two effects excludes zero. The difference needs one shared unit, so it is computed on total cold start; subtracting weight time from compile time would difference two different quantities. The headline rule, lead with what transfers furthest to other infrastructure, was committed before data.
decisions.cost: Total time is noisier than the mechanism units, so the interval is wide: −10.39 s, 95% [−20.30, −5.54]. The pre-registration requires it reported before any ranking claim.
decisions.why_short: "Compile cache mattered more" is a finding only if the gap between the two effects excludes zero.
decisions.cost_short: Total time is noisy, so the interval is wide and the ranking claim must always carry it.

serves.because: R3: "cache X matters more" needs its own interval, "not two point estimates side by side"; the decision rejects "Compare the two point estimates".
R4 fixes the headline rule in advance; here "the headline rule ... was committed before data".

uses.because: The chosen option bootstraps "the difference of contrasts on total cold start".
The pre-registration requires the difference's interval to be "reported before any ranking claim is made".

decisions.title: Report the shape, and what it cannot answer
decisions.problem: Cold starts have a heavy right tail, and 100 runs per arm cannot support every summary.
options: Drop the host hypothesis (H4) quietly once every run lands on one host
p50, p90, p95 and a full ECDF, no p99, and H4 reported as unanswerable
decisions.chosen: p50, p90, p95 and a full ECDF, no p99, and H4 reported as unanswerable
decisions.why: A mean is pulled by the tail. At 100 runs a p99 is one or two observations, not an estimate. Before the published campaign began (a discarded window had already shown runs piling onto one host), the pre-registration committed to publishing the host count whatever it was. The same single host made every triple host-complete, so the paired check is fully supplied.
decisions.cost: The far tail stays unresolved: the post can say that B's largest runs were longer than A's, but not why. The question of whether host placement drives the tail is lost.
decisions.why_short: A mean hides the tail, and at 100 runs a p99 would be one or two observations.
decisions.cost_short: The far tail stays unresolved, and whether host placement drives it is unanswered.
decisions.short: Report the shape and its limits

serves.because: R3: "a mean describes no real run"; the decision: "A mean is pulled by the tail", so it reports p50, p90, p95 and a full ECDF.
R4 fixes the hypotheses in advance; so H4 is reported as unanswerable, and the option to drop it "quietly once every run lands on one host" is rejected.

uses.because: The chosen option is "p50, p90, p95 and a full ECDF, no p99".
It reports H4, whether host placement drives the tail, as unanswerable.

results.title: Where each arm's median cold start goes

deltas.text: Only the weight cache changes. The launch segment falls from 45.83 to 30.35 s (vLLM's own loading time, 17.40 to 4.57 s); compile stays near 19 s.

Only the compile cache changes. Compile nearly vanishes, 18.79 to 0.33 s. But the launch segment also shrank, 30.35 to 21.34 s, with vLLM's own loading time unchanged (4.57 vs 4.54 s); this campaign does not explain why.

results.axis: Median seconds per phase, 100 runs per arm. Each segment is its own median, so bars do not sum to the median totals (81.12, 65.43 and 39.37 s).
results.read_as: The launch segment (the post's `T_weights`) runs from starting `vllm serve` to its "Model loading took" line, so it also holds process start-up. Graph capture's median is 4 s in every arm (vLLM logs it in whole seconds, almost always 4 or 5); it barely differs between arms.
results.takeaway: Each cache shrinks the phase it acts on: weights the launch segment, compile the compile segment. One segment moved that should not have: C also reaches "model loaded" sooner than B.

results.title: The two effects, each measured on its own
results.axis: Median seconds of total cold start each cache saves (the two contrasts).
results.read_as: Side by side these do not rank the caches; the next chart does. Only 18.46 s of the compile cache's 26.07 s is compilation; most of the rest matches the unexplained launch-segment gap above.
results.takeaway: Each cache saves time on its own, roughly 16 s for weights and 26 s for compile; these are context, not the ranking.

results.title: Which cache bought more: the interval on the difference
results.axis: Weight-cache saving minus compile-cache saving: seconds of total cold start, 95% bootstrap interval.
results.read_as: The whole interval, −20.30 to −5.54 s, lies left of zero: the compile cache saves about 10 s more per cold start. That is what licenses the ranking; the pre-registration requires this interval before any ranking claim.
results.takeaway: The compile cache saves more, about 10 s per cold start, and the interval never crosses zero, so the ranking is a finding, not a reading of two bars.

results.title: KV cache left for serving, by arm
results.axis: KV cache tokens vLLM allocated at startup, same card and flags in every arm.
results.read_as: C keeps 20.3 % more KV cache: one more concurrent request at 8192 context (5 instead of 4). On a cold arm the compiler's working set is resident while vLLM measures free memory, so the cache is sized smaller for the replica's life. Pre-registered as H5.
results.takeaway: B and C differ only in the compile cache, yet C gets 20.3 % more KV cache: one more concurrent request, for the replica's whole life.

interview.pitch30: I measured where the time goes when a vLLM server starts cold on a rented GPU, and which of two caches is worth warming: the model weights or the engine's compiled code. I ran three set-ups differing in one thing only, interleaved, a hundred times each, and split every start into phases. The compile cache bought more than the weight cache, and it also left more memory for serving.
interview.pitch120: Everyone talks about caching the weights. But vLLM also compiles parts of the model at startup and caches that on disk, and that second cache is almost invisible unless you have operated the engine. So I asked which one matters more. I set up three arms that differ only in cache configuration: nothing cached, weights on a network volume, and weights plus a warm compile cache. I ran them as shuffled triples so platform drift could not pose as an arm effect, and I wrote down the hypotheses, the exclusion rules and how I would pick the headline before the first paid measurement run. The measuring code ran the real `vllm serve` and read its log, with one clock inside the worker and one on my laptop, so everything outside the worker clock, platform start-up included, is a named residual, not hidden. The answer: warming the compile cache saved about 10 seconds more per cold start than caching the weights, and the interval on that difference never crossed zero. It also left about a fifth more KV cache, because profiling no longer ran next to the compiler's memory. What it cannot tell you is anything about other hardware, or whether host placement drives the tail: every run landed on one machine, and I reported that rather than dropping the question.

followups.q: Why three arms and not two, or four?
followups.a: Two arms (hub vs volume) only test the weight cache, and that was the fallback if this vLLM had not compiled at startup; it does. A to B isolates weights, B to C isolates compile with weights held fixed. The fourth cell, weights cold but compile warm, has no operational meaning. A baked-image arm would just move the bytes into the image pull, which I cannot observe.

The git timestamp is the only evidence that the hypotheses and the headline rule came before the data. It was committed four days before the published campaign's first run, about three before the discarded first window. Later amendments are dated: after that window, the image re-pins and the H4 host-count commitment; after the campaign began, the first-touch separation rule (about half an hour after window one showed a 2174 s platform time; flat-warmup note in the same commit), the window-spacing note and the stopping decision. None changed a hypothesis or a contrast.

Two things. C reached "model loaded" 8.85 s sooner than B, on arms that differ only in compile cache. It is not in vLLM's own model-loading time, which is the same in B and C (4.57 vs 4.54 s): the gap opens before loading begins; not host, not position in the triple, and this campaign does not explain it. And "ready is not fast" was wrong here: vLLM does its warmup before answering health, so the first request is already near steady state.

What the record flags. The host question failed: a serially-submitting driver kept landing on the one machine that had the image cached, and no endpoint setting changes that. The windows were hours apart, not separate days. And the first window was thrown out because arm A's per-run weights filled the worker disk, so A failed 3 of its 9 runs, B none, which would have biased the contrast by survivorship; the worker now empties cold directories before and after each run.

followups.q: What does this not tell you?
followups.a: The seconds for any other GPU, model, engine version, region or provider. Anything about many replicas starting at once and contending for the same volume; every run was one replica alone. Anything past p95. And whether host placement drives the tail.

followups.q: So should everyone warm the compile cache?
followups.a: It is the better buy and the more fragile one. It costs nothing to store, but any change to engine version, model, hardware or flags invalidates it, so every upgrade pays the cold compile again unless warming is built into the deploy. The weight cache is a volume you rent every month whether you scale or not.

interview.limits: One provider, GPU model, model, engine version, region and host: the seconds do not transfer; the mechanisms do. H4 (does host placement drive the tail?) is unanswerable: all 300 runs landed on one host. Single replica, no contention. No percentile past p95. The first-touch rule that keeps the 2266.6 s run out of the ECDF (it stays in the medians) was written after seeing the data and is disclosed as post hoc. Why C reaches "model loaded" 8.85 s sooner than B is not settled.

recall.q: Why are there three arms and not four?
recall.a: The fourth cell, weights cold with compile warm, has no operational meaning, so measuring it fills a table without answering a question. A baked-image arm was also excluded: it moves the weight bytes into the image pull, which is inside the platform residual the harness cannot see.

recall.q: B and C differ only in the compile cache. Which chart segment should change, and which other one changed?
recall.a: Only the compile segment should move, and it does: 18.79 to 0.33 s. The launch segment also shrank, 30.35 to 21.34 s, although vLLM's own loading time is the same in B and C (4.57 vs 4.54 s). The campaign does not explain it, and it is why only 18.46 s of the compile cache's 26.07 s saving is compilation.

recall.q: On the one-run view, where does clock B start, and what lands in platform time?
recall.a: Between steps 4 and 5: the probe starts clock B just before it launches `vllm serve`. Everything the laptop clock sees outside clock B is platform time: queueing, finding a GPU, starting the container and the handler's set-up before it, and teardown and the driver's 5 s polling after it.

recall.q: Why is arm C primed outside the campaign?
recall.a: Otherwise its early runs compile cold and its later runs do not, making the arm a mixture whose effect grows with run index and looks like a trend.

recall.q: Why is the compile cache checked before the engine starts, not after?
recall.a: A cold compile creates the cache directory as it finishes. Checked afterwards, every healthy cold run would look warm and be discarded, and a cold compile inside arm C would pass as warm.

recall.q: How is a contrast obtained, and why does the ranking need a third number?
recall.a: Subtract the medians of two arms that differ in one cache, with a seeded bootstrap interval: A minus B for the weight cache, B minus C for the compile cache. Which cache saves more is a claim about their difference, (A minus B) minus (B minus C), so it needs its own interval, on one shared unit: total cold start. Weight time minus compile time would difference two different quantities.

recall.q: If the difference's interval had run from −20 to +3 s, what could you claim?
recall.a: Not the ranking: no difference, or a slightly larger weight-cache saving, would still fit, and the design makes the ranking a finding only if the interval excludes zero. Each cache's own saving, with its interval, could still be reported.

recall.q: Which requirement breaks if the arms run in blocks, and what protects it?
recall.a: R2, change exactly one thing. In blocks, time-of-day fleet conditions change along with the cache, so a busy evening is labelled as an arm effect. Interleaved triples protect it, together with one frozen cache configuration (three arms, one variable) and the per-run check of each arm's compile-cache state.

recall.q: Why is a failed run never retried in place?
recall.a: A retry quietly replaces slow or unlucky runs with faster ones and makes the distribution look better than it is. Failures are their own rows and are counted per arm.

recall.q: Why does the warm compile cache leave more KV cache?
recall.a: vLLM sizes the KV cache from free memory measured during a profiling pass. On a cold arm the compiler's working set is resident during that pass, so less memory looks free, and the smaller cache stays for the replica's life.
